strengths: The paper makes a timely and clearly motivated dataset/benchmark contribution for distractor-free novel view synthesis, an area where existing public datasets are very small. DF3DV-1K appears substantially larger and more diverse than RobustNeRF and On-the-go, with 1,048 paired clean/cluttered scenes, 89,924 images, indoor/outdoor coverage, 128 distractor types, and 161 scene themes.

The benchmark is useful and appropriately scoped for a dataset paper: it evaluates 3DGS plus nine recent distractor-free radiance-field methods, reports results across prior benchmarks and the new dataset, and identifies method rankings and difficult scenarios such as semantically similar distractors, fluid distractors, and nighttime scenes.

The data acquisition and curation pipeline is described with reasonable care, including manual scene design, consumer-device capture, COLMAP pose estimation, undistortion, instant-ngp verification, and metadata annotation. The paired clean/cluttered design is particularly valuable for quantitative evaluation.

The curated DF3DV-41 subset is a good idea: it gives the benchmark a scenario-wise diagnostic component rather than only a large aggregate score, making the dataset more informative for method development.

The DI2FIX experiment is a convincing demonstration that the dataset can support learning beyond per-scene optimization. The scale ablation and LPIPS-threshold ablation strengthen the case that the dataset’s size and diversity matter.
weaknesses: For a dataset/benchmark paper, reproducibility and release details are under-specified in the main manuscript. I did not see a clear dataset URL, license, code/evaluation-server plan, train/test split files, privacy/consent handling, or long-term hosting commitment. These details are central to assessing the impact of a dataset contribution.

Several benchmark details are deferred to the supplement or only briefly described: how train/test views are chosen per scene, whether methods are tuned uniformly, exact hyperparameter settings, runtime/resource normalization, failure handling, and whether all methods use identical poses and image preprocessing. This makes it hard to fully judge fairness and reproducibility from the main paper alone.

The clean/cluttered separation for uncontrollable scenes is manually performed, but the paper does not quantify annotation reliability, disagreement resolution, or possible residual distractors in the clean set. Since the benchmark relies on clean images as ground truth, this is an important source of noise.

The aggregate benchmark results are valuable, but statistical uncertainty is not reported. With 1,048 scenes, confidence intervals, per-scene distributions, or significance tests would help distinguish small differences among top methods, especially where PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS gaps are modest.

DI2FIX is useful as an application, but it is a 2D post-processing enhancer and may hallucinate or change static scene content. The paper acknowledges some failure cases, but it does not evaluate multi-view consistency, geometry preservation, or downstream artifacts, so the evidence for it as a general solution is limited.

The manuscript would benefit from a stronger societal/privacy discussion. The dataset contains casually captured indoor/outdoor imagery from many scenes and consumer devices; potential privacy filtering, face/license-plate/object removal policies, and distribution restrictions are not discussed in sufficient detail.

strengths: The paper targets a real gap for distractor-free novel view synthesis: existing public datasets such as RobustNeRF and On-the-go are small, and a larger paired clean/cluttered benchmark would be useful to the community if released and maintained.

The claimed scale is substantial for this niche: 1,048 scenes, 89,924 images, indoor/outdoor coverage, 128 distractor types, and a curated 41-scene stress-test subset. The paper also benchmarks a broad set of recent radiance-field/3DGS methods rather than only proposing a dataset in isolation.

The manuscript includes some useful scenario-level analysis, identifying semantically similar distractors, fluid distractors, and nighttime scenes as difficult cases, which could help guide future method development.

The DI2FIX pilot experiment is a reasonable demonstration that the dataset might support learning-based improvements beyond per-scene optimization, and the ablations on data scale and LPIPS filtering are directionally informative.
weaknesses: I assess this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution. Under that standard, the largest weakness is reproducibility and release readiness: the manuscript does not provide a clear dataset URL, license, access protocol, benchmark server, train/test split files, annotation format, privacy policy, or long-term maintenance plan. For a dataset paper, these are central parts of the contribution rather than administrative details.

The data governance discussion is seriously underdeveloped. The dataset includes indoor/outdoor scenes and distractors such as passers-by, vehicles, hands/fingers, and daily scenes, but the paper does not discuss consent, face/license-plate handling, location privacy, removal requests, or whether images with identifiable people are filtered or blurred. This is a consequential omission for a large real-world visual dataset.

The benchmark protocol may leak information from the clean target domain: camera poses are estimated jointly from clean and cluttered images, then used for benchmarking. If methods are supposed to synthesize clean views from cluttered captures, using clean images during pose estimation can make the benchmark less realistic and can change the difficulty in a way that is not quantified. The paper should compare against poses estimated only from cluttered inputs or justify why joint pose estimation is acceptable.

The ground-truth pairing assumptions are not sufficiently validated. For uncontrolled scenes, clean and cluttered images are captured together and later manually separated; even with short capture times, lighting, clouds, moving shadows, and static-scene changes can create mismatches. The paper acknowledges slight cloud movement only in the limitations but does not quantify alignment/temporal consistency errors or their effect on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS.

The quality-control pipeline is vague for a benchmark of this size. It says two experts review scenes and instant-ngp is used for verification, but gives no inter-annotator agreement, rejection statistics, COLMAP failure rates, scene discard counts, annotation taxonomy details, or audit samples. This makes it hard to judge whether the claimed 128 distractor types and 161 themes are consistently labeled.

The experimental evidence relies heavily on aggregate metrics and claims that lower PSNR/SSIM and higher LPIPS prove greater difficulty. Some of this may reflect dataset differences unrelated to distractors, such as camera path, image resolution, scene scale, exposure changes, or pose quality. A stronger benchmark paper would isolate distractor difficulty more carefully, for example with controlled clean-only baselines, pose-error analysis, and per-factor stratification.

The DI2FIX contribution is less convincing than the dataset claim. It is essentially fine-tuning an existing 2D enhancer, and the evaluation averages over renderings from methods also used to construct training pairs. Although a leave-one-method-out test is mentioned, the supporting details are relegated to supplementary tables not present in the main manuscript, and the method may simply learn benchmark-specific restoration priors rather than a robust 3D solution.

Several important implementation details are deferred to supplemental material: benchmark settings, method hyperparameters, DI2FIX details, scenario-wise tables, and OOD evaluation. Since these details determine fairness and reproducibility, the main paper does not provide enough information to independently assess the scientific case.

The paper’s framing is sometimes overstated. Statements such as rankings following publication timeline as evidence of benchmark reliability are weak; publication date is not a principled validation criterion. Similarly, “zoom-in no more” qualitative comparison is rhetorically appealing but not a rigorous benchmark property.

Overall, the idea is valuable, but the current submission does not yet make a sufficiently convincing, reproducible, and ethically documented case for acceptance as a dataset/benchmark paper. The missing release/governance/protocol details are central enough that I would lean against acceptance despite the apparent scale of the collection.

strengths: I assess this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, with a secondary applied component through DI2FIX. Under that lens, the core contribution is substantial: DF3DV-1K provides 1,048 real scenes, 89,924 images, paired clean/cluttered captures, indoor/outdoor coverage, 128 distractor types, and 161 scene themes, which is a clear scale and diversity jump over RobustNeRF and On-the-go.

The paper targets a timely and well-motivated gap in distractor-free novel view synthesis. The motivation is convincing: existing public benchmarks are small and increasingly saturated, making it hard to distinguish recent methods without subtle qualitative zoom-ins.

The data collection and curation pipeline is thoughtfully described, including controlled and uncontrolled capture, manual quality review, COLMAP-based shared pose estimation, undistortion, instant-ngp verification, and metadata annotation. The inclusion of DF3DV-41 as a curated hard subset across 17 scenarios is especially useful for diagnosing failure modes rather than only reporting averages.

The benchmark is broad and valuable, evaluating 3DGS plus nine recent distractor-free radiance-field methods across DF3DV-1K, DF3DV-41, On-the-go, and RobustNeRF. This should be useful to the community even if no new reconstruction algorithm were proposed.

The analysis goes beyond leaderboard reporting by identifying challenging categories such as semantically similar distractors, fluid distractors, and nighttime scenes, and by comparing how dataset rankings differ from previous benchmarks.

The DI2FIX experiment is a good demonstration that the dataset can support learning-based progress beyond per-scene optimization. The reported gains over vanilla renderings and over non-domain-tuned DIFIX support the claim that the dataset has training value, not only evaluation value.

The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and well situated in the recent literature. The figures and tables communicate the dataset scale, capture process, and benchmark outcomes effectively.
weaknesses: The strongest reservation is reproducibility and release detail. The main paper does not clearly specify the concrete release plan, license, access conditions, code/evaluation scripts, benchmark server, or data card/documentation. For a dataset/benchmark paper, acceptance should depend on these artifacts being available and usable.

Several important protocol details appear to be deferred to the supplement, including method-specific settings, train/test splits, benchmark averaging, and scenario-wise tables. The main paper would be stronger if it included enough detail to judge whether all compared methods were tuned and run fairly, especially given the very large compute budget and rapid evolution of the evaluated methods.

The clean/cluttered pairing is valuable but also raises possible evaluation noise: uncontrolled scenes are separated manually after capture, and clean captures may still contain cloud movement or other residual changes. The paper acknowledges slight cloud movement but does not quantify annotation/label noise, inter-annotator agreement, or the frequency of residual distractors and scene changes.

The benchmark relies heavily on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS against clean views. These are standard, but for distractor removal they may not fully capture whether static scene content is preserved versus hallucinated or over-smoothed. More targeted metrics, human preference studies, or mask/category-conditioned evaluation would strengthen the scientific case.

DI2FIX is useful as a proof of dataset utility, but it is a 2D post-enhancer rather than a geometrically consistent radiance-field method. It may hallucinate or modify static content, and the comparisons are limited mainly to DIFIX variants rather than a broader set of restoration/enhancement baselines.

The paper does not discuss privacy, consent, or anonymization for large-scale casual indoor/outdoor imagery, which may include people, homes, vehicles, signs, or other identifying content. This is a notable omission for a large real-world dataset paper.

Some claims are a bit overstated, such as treating alignment with publication timeline as evidence of benchmark reliability. This is suggestive but not a rigorous validation of benchmark quality, and could also reflect implementation maturity, hyperparameter tuning, or method selection bias.
